summary:
The Bahamas decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 16 May 1991 through the Sexual Offences and Domestic Violence Act. Nothing in the sources indicates that a visitor can be prosecuted for consensual sexual conduct, and no pattern of police targeting of visitors for sexual conduct is documented.

Transgender and intersex residents and visitors hold no statutory protection. Bahamas Transgender, Intersex United stated this absence plainly when it launched the 'Bahamian Trans Lives Matter' campaign in April 2016, and member Torri Culmer has advocated against job termination for trans and intersex workers. The gap is statutory, not merely administrative: no enacted non-discrimination provision covering gender identity appears anywhere in the sources, and the Constitution's prohibition against discrimination does not extend to sexual orientation or gender identity. The 2006 Constitutional Reform Commission did not regard sexual orientation as deserving protection, and efforts to include it in a proposed constitution were blocked by members citing religious opposition.

Official statements point in two directions. In May 1998 National Security Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Frank Watson announced that the military, prison service and police do not discriminate on the basis of sexual orientation, and LGBT citizens face no prohibition on serving in those forces. Against that, government officials have opposed LGBT rights: former Prime Minister Perry Christie stated in 2013 that he did not believe in same-sex marriage and said in 2016 that a referendum would not legalise it, defining marriage as between male and female determined at birth. Government member Leslie Miller publicly called for the 'Exile of Transgender out of the Bahamas,' urging financial contributions to relocate transgender people to a private island and pledging $1,000 toward it.

Same-sex marriage and civil unions are not legal. The Marriage Act defines marriage as between a man and a woman, same-sex households are denied the rights given to opposite-sex married couples, and in 2011 former Minister of State Zhivargo Laing stated that a marriage is void if between persons of the same sex, describing this as a community standard. The 2016 referendum bills were not inclusive of transgender or intersex people.

Statutory protection remains narrow. The Data Protection (Privacy of Personal Information) Act 2003 lists 'sexual life' as sensitive personal data, and a 2001 Employment Bill clause banning sexual-orientation workplace discrimination was removed shortly after passage. There are no national hate-crime laws, and discrimination in healthcare or education on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity is not illegal. No HIV-specific or trans-specific care provisions are recorded.

The criminal code sets the age of consent at 16 for heterosexual acts and 18 for same-sex acts. The Communications Act 2009 empowers URCA to issue codes of practice against content likely to incite hatred or vilify persons on the basis of sexual preference.

Violence against LGBT people is documented. In May 2017 Adrian Brown, 24, Jamaica-born and US-resident, was treated at Doctors Hospital for a head laceration after being targeted and beaten because he is gay at Bahamas Junkanoo Carnival, and he wants charges laid. A 2009 murder victim, a homosexual HIV-positive man, was killed by a defendant acquitted using a 'gay panic' defence, and nine murders of gay men between 2001 and 2015 remain unsolved. In 2005 an 18-year-old beauty queen had her crown stripped after confirming she was a lesbian.

Social hostility is substantial and shapes the visitor environment. Surveys record 85.5% strongly disapproving of same-sex marriage in 2015 with 10.6% approving, and over 84% strongly disapproving of a gay or lesbian politician in 2013 with 12% positive. Many Bahamians belong to conservative Christian denominations treating homosexuality and cross-dressing as decadence, and politicians have been leery of publicly supporting LGBT-rights legislation. In 2016 the Canadian government issued travel advice warning gay couples about the risk of homophobia in the Bahamas.

There are no exclusively gay bars or clubs; the Nassau scene is underground, and LGBT groups are often pressured to keep social events hidden. Police raided a gay party in downtown Nassau on 6 October 2007 with no arrests, and the Ministry of Tourism later apologised. Groups of LGBT tourists have been protested, including church group opposition to Rosie O'Donnell's 2004 cruise and a 1998 protest against a lesbian cruise; in September 2007 the Bahamas Christian Council formed an anti-gay committee over a request to a local cable company to carry the LGBTQ channel Logo. The Plays and Films Control Board banned Brokeback Mountain in March 2006 and attempted to block a public-square screening of Children of God on 24 June 2011, though the government overruled it.
tangentialFactors:
The Bahamas presents a mixed legal picture that a trans visitor should read as a whole: consensual same-sex conduct is decriminalised and an official 1998 statement asserts non-discrimination in the security services, but there is no enacted protection on gender identity, no hate-crime law, and no marriage or partnership recognition for same-sex couples.

Public opinion and organised religious opposition are the main drivers of the social environment rather than criminal law. The gap between the 1998 ministerial statement and the 2016 call by a government member to exile transgender people illustrates how official positions have diverged over two decades.

Violence documented in the sources targets gay men specifically; no incident involving a trans visitor is recorded, so the trans-specific violence risk is not directly sourced even though the hostile climate is.

outOfScopeNotes:
The sources do not record any rule governing the amendment of gender markers on Bahamian passports or identity documents, nor any entry or visa screening that could disclose a visitor's trans status. This is an absence in the inventory, not a finding that no such rule exists.

No source states whether a trans visitor's entry, visa, or customs screening would be affected by gender presentation, and no source addresses which foreign documents the Bahamas recognises for gender marker purposes.

The sources record violence against gay men but no documented incident involving a trans visitor; the trans-specific violence risk in practice is therefore not directly sourced.

Whether the 1998 non-discrimination statement by Frank Watson has any binding effect, and whether any enforcement mechanism exists behind it, is not resolved by the inventory.
